name: Diabolical Conspiracy and Collective Guilt
primary_locale: All European prosecution territories; especially central to German-speaking and Francophone prosecution
scholarly_definition: The concept of diabolical conspiracy addresses both the demonological doctrine — formulated explicitly by the mid-fifteenth century — that witches were not isolated individuals who had made individual compacts with the devil but members of a coordinated collective conspiracy, and the modern analytical framework identifying that doctrine's role in enabling mass prosecution. In demonological doctrine, the conspiracy constituted a counter-church or anti-society organized under Satan's leadership, meeting at sabbaths to renew collective allegiance, practicing collective ritual inversion of Christian worship, and coordinating mass maleficium against the Christian community. This collectivization of the witch's identity was the doctrinal innovation that made mass prosecution logically possible: if witches were organized conspirators, then any convicted witch was necessarily connected to other members of the conspiracy whose identities she could reveal through interrogation-induced denunciation. As a hybrid term, 'diabolical conspiracy' names both the contemporaries' own demonological doctrine — the 'sect of witches' or 'synagogue of Satan' — and the modern analytical category identifying that doctrine's role in generating denunciation cascades and mass prosecution episodes. Norman Cohn's Europe's Inner Demons (1975) is the foundational modern analysis, arguing that the conspiracy-sect stereotype was not a response to actual witch practices but a projection onto accused witches of the same accusations of secret nocturnal assembly, blasphemy, infanticide, and sexual deviance that had earlier been directed at heretics (Cathars, Waldensians), Jews, and early Christians. In Cohn's analysis, the conspiracy stereotype was a fantasy produced by the prosecutorial imagination rather than a distorted reflection of actual practice.

intellectual_genealogy.cohn_europes_inner_demons_1975: Norman Cohn, Europe's Inner Demons (1975), is the foundational scholarly analysis of the diabolical conspiracy stereotype, tracing its genealogy from ancient accusations against early Christians through medieval heresy accusations to the crystallization of the witch-conspiracy doctrine in the fifteenth century.
intellectual_genealogy.early_fifteenth_century_crystallization: The collective conspiracy doctrine crystallized in the period c. 1430–1460, visible in early Alpine and Savoyard trial records and in the earliest comprehensive demonological treatises (Johannes Nider's Formicarius, c. 1437; the Errores Gazariorum, c. 1437; Claude Tholosan's Ut magorum et maleficiorum errores, c. 1436). Ginzburg's Night Battles and Ecstasies trace the formation of the composite stereotype in this period.
intellectual_genealogy.malleus_maleficarum_consolidation: The Malleus Maleficarum (1487) consolidated the collective conspiracy doctrine in print, providing the fully elaborated framework in which individual maleficium, demonic pact, and sabbath conspiracy were integrated into a single demonological composite that shaped subsequent European prosecution.
intellectual_genealogy.denunciation_mechanism: The doctrinal collectivism of the conspiracy model created the procedural denunciation mechanism that drove mass prosecution episodes: each confessing witch was expected to name accomplices from the conspiracy, whose subsequent interrogation produced further names, generating the cascade dynamic that Brian Levack and others analyze as the primary engine of mass prosecution.

clark_intellectual_analysis: Clark analyzes the collective conspiracy concept as structurally integrated with the inversion principle and the logic of the demonic mirror-society: the witches' conspiracy was the systematic inversion of Christian society, organized on the same hierarchical, sacramental, and communal lines but in the service of the devil rather than God. This inversion logic made the conspiracy concept intellectually coherent — if Christian society had its church, its sacraments, its community worship, and its hierarchy, the devil's counter-society would have its sabbath, its mock-sacraments, its collective gathering, and its infernal hierarchy.
hutton_social_analysis: The collective conspiracy concept explains, for Hutton, why denunciation cascades occurred: each confessing witch named accomplices who were members of the same conspiracy, and the prosecution's logical obligation to identify and remove all conspiracy members produced the expansion dynamic that transformed individual prosecutions into mass trials. Hutton also notes that the conspiracy model interacted with community-level social dynamics, since the named accomplices were typically drawn from the accused's actual social network — creating a feedback loop in which the conspiracy model shaped prosecution in ways that reflected genuine community relationships.
ginzburg_interrogation_analysis: Ginzburg's recovery of genuine popular traditions raises the foundational question about the conspiracy stereotype: if the benandanti and comparable traditions involved genuine communal spirit-contact practices, what (if anything) was the collective conspiracy doctrine distorting or overlaying? Ginzburg's answer — that the conspiracy stereotype was the learned framework imposed on popular spirit-contact traditions rather than a complete fantasy — distinguishes his position from Cohn's pure fantasy model while accepting that the conspiracy stereotype as elaborated in demonological doctrine exceeded anything in the popular traditions themselves.

actor_perspective.demonological_vocabulary_for_conspiracy: Contemporary demonological literature described the witch conspiracy using the vocabulary of heresy and treason: the 'sect of witches' (secta strigiarum), the 'synagogue of Satan', the 'congregation of the devil', the 'assembly of malefactors'. These terms located the conspiracy within the established categories of collective religious deviance (heretical sect) and political crime (conspiracy against the sovereign).
actor_perspective.confessing_witches_collective_testimony: Accused persons who confessed under torture or its threat were expected to name accomplices from the conspiracy — 'who else was at the sabbath?' being the standard interrogator's follow-up question. Many confessions contain lists of named accomplices, drawn from the accused's actual community, that reflect the conspiracy doctrine's demand for collective guilt while also reflecting genuine social networks.
actor_perspective.judicial_and_theological_authorities: Prosecutors and demonologists understood the conspiracy model as providing both the legal justification for demanding denunciation (each accused person was a witness to the conspiracy and legally obligated to name fellow conspirators) and the theological rationale for unlimited prosecution (the conspiracy extended as far as the devil's reach, which was everywhere).

geographic_distribution: The diabolical conspiracy doctrine was central to mass prosecution in German-speaking territories (Bamberg, Würzburg, Trier, southwestern Germany generally), in Francophone territories (Lorraine, Franche-Comté, some Swiss cantons), and in the early Alpine trials from which the stereotype crystallized. English prosecution showed a comparatively weaker conspiracy emphasis, with individual maleficium accusations more common than full conspiracy-based mass trials. Spanish and Italian inquisitorial courts were often skeptical of the conspiracy model, limiting their prosecution accordingly.
historiographical_significance: The diabolical conspiracy concept is historiographically central because it provides the doctrinal mechanism that transformed witch prosecution from a series of isolated individual trials into the mass persecution episodes that define the 'witch hunt' in popular memory and scholarly analysis. Without the conspiracy doctrine's logic — each witch is connected to other members of an organized sect whose identities she can reveal — the denunciation cascades that produced mass prosecution episodes in Germany and elsewhere would have had no doctrinal justification. Cohn's genealogical analysis of the conspiracy stereotype, connecting it to earlier accusations against heretics and Jews, situates the witch hunt within the longer history of European religious persecution and challenges any analysis that treats witch prosecution as a unique or sui generis phenomenon. Ginzburg's counter-argument — that the conspiracy stereotype overlaid genuine popular traditions rather than being pure fantasy — represents the most important challenge to Cohn's analysis and remains the primary axis of the major interpretive debate in the field.
source_method: Norman Cohn, Europe's Inner Demons (1975); Stuart Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997/2001); Ronald Hutton, The Witch (2017); H.C. Erik Midelfort, Witch-Hunting in Southwestern Germany (1972); early fifteenth-century Alpine trial records analyzed by Cohn, Ginzburg, and Levack
scholarly_disagreement: The fundamental debate is between Cohn's 'pure fantasy' model and Ginzburg's 'distorted popular tradition' model. Cohn argues that the collective conspiracy stereotype was entirely a projection of the prosecutorial imagination onto accused persons, with no genuine popular practice underlying it. Ginzburg argues that the stereotype overlaid and distorted genuine popular traditions of communal spirit-contact and night-journey practice, making it a hybrid of learned fantasy and popular substrate. Hutton accepts Ginzburg's evidence for specific documented cases (benandanti, Thiess) while questioning whether it supports the broad comparative synthesis. Levack occupies a middle position: accepting that the conspiracy model was primarily a doctrinal construction while acknowledging that some popular communal magical practices may have provided partial raw material for its elaboration. The debate about whether any real communal practice underlies the conspiracy stereotype remains unresolved and is one of the field's central open questions.
